<reason>Side A won a clear but competitive debate. A built three durable routes: scale economies on high-fixed-cost goods, missing-supply (childcare/transit deserts) that cash cannot summon into existence, and risk-pooling for catastrophic need. B's strongest pressure—heterogeneous needs, government failure, and the charge that A "retreated" to cancer care—was partially effective, and B's answer that subsidized insurance differs from government-run services was genuinely clever. But A's counter was decisive: insurance is earmarked, pooled, restricted spending, so B repeatedly answered every concrete need with a non-cash mechanism (insurance, co-ops, sitters, ride-pools), conceding A's principle in practice; and insurance cannot pay out a daycare that does not exist. Since healthcare is explicitly in the motion, B's "narrow edge case" framing lost force. A also landed a clean decision rule—cash is only as good as the market beneath it; services win exactly where the market fails—and A's political-durability and spillover points were never answered. B's rigidity examples were vivid but met with plausible "design parameter" responses, leaving that clash a wash. A's closings and pressure questions were sharper and better crystallized the choice.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was the insurance clash: B's pressure question distinguishing risk-pooled insurance from government-operated services was answered by A's A4.1-A4.3, which framed insurance as earmarked collective provision (conceding the proposition's principle) and noted that pooling cannot create missing supply in a desert—a point B never fully neutralized, only reframed.</best_rebuttal>
